doc.title: Ingrid Sertso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, August 11, 2014

title: Writing new lyrics for Ornette's Lonely Woman; Ornette keeps them in America
summary: Ornette liked her lyrics; he played the recording seven times and is her guru. Early US shocks made them want to leave, but Ornette made them stay.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: And being a poet, have you set any of your poems to melodies?

Yes, yes. I just did “Lonely Woman” by Ornette Coleman. And Ornette never liked the lyrics. They were done by a poet he never got introduced to, by a woman. And he said, “That’s not what my song is about.” And Ornette and me, we just keep talking together. And so I called him and said, “Ornette, can I write some lyrics for ‘Lonely Woman’ and come down and show them to you and then record it? He said, “You just write it, you don’t have to come down, record it and bring me the recording.” Because he knows my poetry. And it’s on my last CD, “Lonely Woman.” And we went there, Karl and me. Ornette put it on seven times. I was so honored. Because I adore him so much. Of all the

musicians in this country, it’s Ornette is like a guru to us. He’s like a guru. He kept us. We wanted to leave the second week we came here. Because when you come from Europe all these musicians they come from here are superstars there. They are honored. People go to the concerts. People put extra dress on, extra suit. And then you come over here. The first experience was a very famous musician, I don’t want to mention his name, a saxophone player, came over and asked Karl for a few dollars so he can buy a new mouthpiece. For us the world broke down. I went to Copacabana club because Anita O’Day was one of my favorite white singers. She sat at the bar and cried. I said to the waiter, “What’s happening?” And he said, “She came late, she is fired.” So it was one experience like the other and so we wanted to go back because we felt this we can’t deal with. Ornette was the one that said no. He knew our music. He had already come to quite a few concerts after a few months. We immediately linked up with club managers and he came to almost every concert when he was younger. And he loved it and he said, “No, you stay in this country.” He’s the one that made us stay.
